title: Paraguay's ousted President Peña moved to a military prison over the Ueno Bank collapse
seoTitle: Paraguay: Peña in military prison over Ueno Bank collapse
dek: The Senate removed Santiago Peña on 6 November after Ueno Bank, a digital lender holding public and pension money, collapsed. A judge ordered him moved to the Viñas Cue military prison on 16 November after reports of special comforts in custody. He denies wrongdoing.
happened: Paraguay's central bank took over the digital lender Ueno Bank after its solvency fell below the legal minimum, and operations stopped nationwide. The bank had about 3 million customers and more than $800 million in public money. On 5 November President Santiago Peña announced his resignation, but a joint session of Congress to consider it lacked a quorum, and the Chamber of Deputies approved impeachment charges 78 to 0. On 6 November the Senate found him guilty of poor performance of his duties: all 44 senators present voted to remove him, with one of 45 absent. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in to serve until August 2028. That evening prosecutors placed Peña under house arrest in Asunción, and he appeared before them on the morning of 7 November. He is the second Paraguayan president removed by impeachment since the end of the Stroessner dictatorship in 1989; the first was Fernando Lugo in 2012. Crowds outside Congress cheered the verdict, and protesters marched through central Asunción and gathered outside Peña's home. On 16 November, his 48th birthday, Judge Osmar Legal ordered Peña moved from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in Asunción, to the Viñas Cue military prison, to "ensure compliance with the pretrial detention measure". The order followed reports by the newspaper ABC Color that his quarters there included a large dining room, furnishings, a private gym and a private bathroom. He is held apart from other inmates for his safety.

sides.says: In a farewell message he wrote: "I say goodbye with gratitude, without ignoring the anguish of those who are waiting for answers today", and said he did not want his "presence to be a cause of greater division or instability". On social media he wrote: "I want to apologize to the Paraguayan people if I have failed you." He denies wrongdoing and says he sold his stake in the bank's parent company in 2025.

Adolfo Ferreiro and Ricardo Preda asked Congress to accept his resignation and close the trial. Preda argued that the accusation did not identify any illegal order or decision by the president, and that banking supervision and pension fund investments were decisions for the boards of the central bank and the social security institute (IPS).

They accuse Peña of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno Bank and of letting the regulator overlook alleged irregularities in its loans. Opposition deputy Rocío Vallejo, one of the prosecutors, said the central bank gave Ueno "an immediate death sentence" without prior intervention (translated from Spanish).

sides.who: President Pedro Alliana and the Colorado Party
sides.says: On 16 November Alliana said he had dismissed Colonel José David Daiub, who was accused of giving Peña special treatment in detention. He said: "Our priority is to guarantee the country's stability, restore confidence, and provide concrete and rapid solutions", and that Paraguayans "deserve to know the truth". Earlier he said he would act to compensate people who lost money; NPR reported no amount or timetable. He is also under investigation in connection with the bank, AP reports. Before the verdict, former president and party leader Horacio Cartes backed the impeachment and said the party would not side with "the theft of public, private and pension funds".

Prosecutors accuse Peña of using his office to direct public funds to Ueno Bank while it made insider loans to its owners. He faces charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain, and is held in pretrial detention; he has not been convicted. AP reported the most serious offences carry up to 10 years in prison. Prosecutors also ordered the arrest of former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, who ran the finance company that became Ueno until Peña appointed him in 2023. In a separate case 27 people have been charged, including the bank's founder and former CEO, and a judge has sent six former directors into pretrial detention.

Board member Liana Caballero said: "We proceeded to close the entity" (translated from Spanish). The bank says deposits are insured up to about $35,000, which covers 97% of Ueno's customers. Critics say it did not regulate Ueno properly.
Al Jazeera reported on 5 November that the bank had made no public statement.

next: Peña remains in pretrial detention at Viñas Cue while the criminal case continues; no trial date has been reported. Removal costs him the lifetime Senate seat that former presidents receive. Savers began recovering money on 5 November, starting with balances up to 10 million guaraníes, about $1,500, and Law 7745 allows an advance of up to 40 minimum wages, about 121.7 million guaraníes, per saver.
summary: Paraguay's Senate removed President Santiago Peña on 6 November after the collapse of Ueno Bank, a digital lender used by about 3 million people that held roughly $850 million in public funds, including pension money. Prosecutors accuse him of steering public money to the bank; he denies wrongdoing. On 16 November a judge moved him to a military prison after reports of a private gym and other comforts in custody, and President Pedro Alliana dismissed the officer accused of granting them. Savers have begun to recover their deposits.

conflicts: Sources differ on when the central bank acted: ABC Color and RPP date its decision to 2 November; AP and MercoPress report the takeover on Tuesday, 3 November.
Pension institute (IPS) money held at the bank: Infobae says about $380 million; RPP and AP, citing lawmakers, say $355 million.
Ueno's customers: NPR says about 3 million; AP, citing the bank, says about 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there.

Where Peña was held: AP reported on 7 November that prosecutors placed him under house arrest in Asunción; Al Jazeera and Anadolu report that before 16 November he was held in pretrial detention at the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base, and do not mention house arrest.
Public money at the bank: AP reported more than $800 million; Al Jazeera says roughly $850 million.
